title: No one actually justified until the Spirit applies Christ by faith and repentance
source_text: XX. Itaque plane dicendum putamus neminem actu & revera justificatum esse, priusquam Spiritus Sanctus fidem & resipiscentiam in eo creans & excitans, Christum ipsi applicuerit. Quae est expressa sententia Confessionis Anglicanae: Parlamenti, ut vocant, Anglicani, ante aliquot annos authoritate edita. Sic enim habet cap. 11. art. 4. prout ex translatione Gallica vertere licuit, Deus ab aeterno decrevit justificare omnes electos. Et in complemento temporum Christus pro peccatis eorum mortuus est, & propter justificationem eorum resurrexit. Attamen justificati non sunt, donec Spiritus Sanctus illorum unicuique suo tempore Christum reapse applicuerit. Atque idem sentire, si sibi constare velint, necesse est omnes illos qui existimant fidem esse medium cujus interventu justificemur, qui proculdubio longe maximam partem Reformatorum constituunt.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore we plainly think it must be said that no one is actually and truly justified before the Holy Spirit, creating and stirring faith and repentance in him, has applied Christ to him. Which is the express sentence of the Anglican Confession—of the English Parliament, as they call it—published by authority some years ago. For so it has in chapter 11 article 4, as we may render from the French translation: God from eternity decreed to justify all the elect. And in the fullness of time Christ died for their sins and rose again for their justification. Yet they are not justified until the Holy Spirit has in his time actually applied Christ to each of them. And all those who think faith is the means by whose intervention we are justified—who without doubt make up by far the greatest part of the Reformers—must, if they wish to be consistent with themselves, hold the same.
pass_b_english: Actual justification waits until the Spirit applies Christ by creating faith and repentance.
Westminster/Anglican art. and most Reformers who call faith the means agree.

rejected: faith as mere sense of prior decree
